stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Grammatical gender is common among the world's languages. French, German, and Hindi, among many others, assign a gender to every noun ______ Finnish has no grammatical gender at all. Even its single third-person pronoun, hän, is used for both men and women.
explanation: "French, German, and Hindi... assign a gender to every noun" is a complete sentence, and so is "Finnish has no grammatical gender at all." Two complete sentences need a strong break between them, so the semicolon goes after "noun." "However" signals the contrast with Finnish, so it starts the second clause and is followed by a comma.

A.why: You treated "however" like "but" and joined two complete sentences with only commas. That is a comma splice.

C.why: You put no punctuation at all between "noun" and "however," so two complete sentences run together without a break.

D.why: You put the semicolon after "however," which attaches the contrast to the first clause. That clause doesn't contrast with the sentence before it; it gives examples of it. The contrast belongs with Finnish.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For decades, folklorists assumed that the tale of the clever tailor began in Germany, where the Brothers Grimm had recorded a well-known version of it. Recent fieldwork has turned up Persian and Turkish variants that are centuries older than the German one ______ most scholars now place the tale's origin much farther east.
explanation: "Recent fieldwork has turned up... variants that are centuries older than the German one" is a complete sentence, and so is "most scholars now place the tale's origin much farther east." The semicolon goes between them. "Therefore" introduces the result, which is the new view of the tale's origin, so it begins the second clause and takes a comma.

A.why: You treated "therefore" like a conjunction and joined two complete sentences with commas alone. That is a comma splice.

B.why: You left out the break between the two complete sentences, which creates a run-on.

C.why: You put the semicolon after "therefore," which makes the discovery of older variants a result of the earlier assumption. The discovery isn't the result. The scholars' new conclusion is, so "therefore" belongs to the second clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Gerardus Mercator's 1569 world map greatly enlarges regions near the poles. On it, Greenland looks roughly as large as Africa, though Africa is about fourteen times bigger. Cartographers have long criticized this ______ the projection remains standard for nautical charts, because any constant compass bearing appears on it as a straight line.
explanation: "Cartographers have long criticized this distortion" is a complete sentence, and so is "the projection remains standard for nautical charts." Put the semicolon between them. "Even so" says the projection is still used despite the criticism, so it opens the second clause and is followed by a comma.

B.why: You joined two complete sentences with commas alone, as if "even so" were a conjunction. That is a comma splice.

C.why: You put the semicolon after "even so," which ties it to the criticism. That would mean cartographers criticize the map despite its distortion, which makes no sense. The "despite" relationship belongs to the projection's continued use.

D.why: With no punctuation after "distortion," the two complete sentences run together into a run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most young songbirds learn to sing by copying an adult male of their own species. A young brown-headed cowbird, though, hatches in the nest of a warbler or sparrow and never hears an adult cowbird ______ it must develop its song another way: by noticing which notes draw a response from females.
explanation: "A young brown-headed cowbird... never hears an adult cowbird sing" is a complete sentence, and so is "it must develop its song another way." They need a semicolon between them. "Consequently" introduces the result of never hearing an adult cowbird, so it starts the second clause and takes a comma.

A.why: You joined two complete sentences with only commas around "consequently," as though it were "so." That is a comma splice.

B.why: You put no punctuation between the two complete sentences, which creates a run-on.

D.why: You put the semicolon after "consequently," which makes the cowbird's upbringing a result of how other songbirds learn. The result is actually the cowbird's need to learn another way, so "consequently" belongs to that clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Printmaking techniques are often grouped by where the ink sits on the printing surface. Woodcut artists carve away the parts of a block meant to stay blank, leaving raised areas to hold the ______ etchers use acid to bite lines into a metal plate, and the ink collects in those sunken grooves.
explanation: "Woodcut artists carve away... leaving raised areas to hold the ink" is a complete sentence, and so is "etchers use acid to bite lines into a metal plate." The semicolon goes between them. "In contrast" sets etching against woodcut, so it begins the second clause and is followed by a comma.

A.why: You joined two complete sentences with commas alone, as though "in contrast" could link them like "but." That is a comma splice.

C.why: You put the semicolon after "in contrast," which makes woodcut contrast with the opening sentence about how techniques are grouped. Woodcut is one example of that grouping, not a contrast to it. The contrast is etching.

D.why: With no punctuation after "ink," the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on.
